claim: The mouse retina expresses a short wavelength-sensitive opsin (S-opsin) and a middle/long wavelength-sensitive opsin (M-opsin).
source: The mouse retina expresses a short wavelength-sensitive and a middle/long wavelength-sensitive opsin (S- and M-opsin), forming opposing, overlapping gradients along the dorsal-ventral axis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: S-opsin and M-opsin form opposing, overlapping gradients along the dorsal-ventral axis of the mouse retina.
source: The mouse retina expresses a short wavelength-sensitive and a middle/long wavelength-sensitive opsin (S- and M-opsin), forming opposing, overlapping gradients along the dorsal-ventral axis.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: True S-cones (expressing only S-opsin) are highly concentrated in the ventral retina, comprising up to 30% of cones in that region.
source: We found, unexpectedly, that 'true S-cones' (S-opsin only) are highly concentrated (up to 30% of cones) in ventral retina.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by quantitative data in Figure 1C, Figure 2A, and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: True S-cones comprise approximately 1% of cones in the dorsal retina.
source: This result is evident from density maps of cone types from three examples of pigmented mice, showing highly concentrated true S-cones in the ventral retina (Figure 2A, left column, bottom row). In addition, M+S--cones were concentrated in the dorsal retina, whereas mixed cones dominated the medial and ventral retina (Figure 1C left and Figure 2A, left column, 4th and 5th rows).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: S-cone bipolar cells (SCBCs) are skewed towards the ventral retina.
source: Moreover, S-cone bipolar cells (SCBCs) are also skewed towards ventral retina, with wiring patterns matching the distribution of true S-cones.
evidence: This is supported by density maps and quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The wiring patterns of SCBCs match the distribution of true S-cones.
source: Moreover, S-cone bipolar cells (SCBCs) are also skewed towards ventral retina, with wiring patterns matching the distribution of true S-cones.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity analysis shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: True S-cones in the ventral retina form clusters.
source: In addition, true S-cones in the ventral retina form clusters, which may augment synaptic input to SCBCs.
evidence: This is supported by K-nearest neighbor analysis and visualization shown in Figure 4A-B and quantified in Figure 4E.

claim: True S-cone clustering may augment synaptic input to SCBCs.
source: In addition, true S-cones in the ventral retina form clusters, which may augment synaptic input to SCBCs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed clustering pattern and connectivity data.

claim: The unique true S-cone and SCBC connecting pattern forms a basis for mouse color vision.
source: Such a unique true S-cone and SCBC connecting pattern forms a basis for mouse color vision, likely reflecting evolutionary adaptation to enhance color coding for the upper visual field suitable for mice's habitat and behavior.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the anatomical findings and supported by references to behavioral studies.

claim: The true S-cone and SCBC pattern likely reflects evolutionary adaptation to enhance color coding for the upper visual field.
source: Such a unique true S-cone and SCBC connecting pattern forms a basis for mouse color vision, likely reflecting evolutionary adaptation to enhance color coding for the upper visual field suitable for mice's habitat and behavior.
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation based on the anatomical findings.

claim: Color is encoded by comparing signals from photoreceptors with different spectral sensitivities.
source: Color, an important visual cue for survival, is encoded by comparing signals from photoreceptors with different spectral sensitivities.
evidence: This is established knowledge in color vision science, supported by citation (Baden and Osorio, 2019).

claim: S-opsin has peak sensitivity at 360 nm.
source: The mouse retina expresses two types of cone opsins, S- and M-opsin, with peak sensitivities at 360 nm and 508 nm, respectively (Jacobs et al., 1991; Nikonov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Jacobs et al., 1991; Nikonov et al., 2006).

claim: M-opsin has peak sensitivity at 508 nm.
source: The mouse retina expresses two types of cone opsins, S- and M-opsin, with peak sensitivities at 360 nm and 508 nm, respectively (Jacobs et al., 1991; Nikonov et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Jacobs et al., 1991; Nikonov et al., 2006).

claim: A majority of cones in the mouse retina express both S-opsin and M-opsin (mixed cones).
source: The expression patterns of these two opsins form opposing and overlapping gradients along the dorsal-ventral axis, resulting in a majority of cones expressing both opsins (herein either 'mixed cones' or M+S+) (Applebury et al., 2000; Ng et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies (Applebury et al., 2000; Ng et al., 2001; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: S-opsin enrichment in the ventral retina better detects short-wavelength light from the sky.
source: Thus, S-opsin enrichment in the ventral retina better detects short-wavelength light from the sky, and M-opsin in the dorsal retina perceives the ground (e.g., a grassy field) (Baden et al., 2013; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004; Osorio and Vorobyev, 2005; Szél et al., 1992), while co-expression of both opsins (herein either mixed cones or M+S+) (Röhlich et al., 1994) broadens the spectral range of individual cones and improves perception under varying conditions of ambient light (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations (Baden et al., 2013; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004; Osorio and Vorobyev, 2005; Szél et al., 1992).

claim: M-opsin in the dorsal retina perceives the ground.
source: Thus, S-opsin enrichment in the ventral retina better detects short-wavelength light from the sky, and M-opsin in the dorsal retina perceives the ground (e.g., a grassy field) (Baden et al., 2013; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004; Osorio and Vorobyev, 2005; Szél et al., 1992), while co-expression of both opsins (herein either mixed cones or M+S+) (Röhlich et al., 1994) broadens the spectral range of individual cones and improves perception under varying conditions of ambient light (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations (Baden et al., 2013; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004; Osorio and Vorobyev, 2005; Szél et al., 1992).

claim: Co-expression of both opsins broadens the spectral range of individual cones and improves perception under varying conditions of ambient light.
source: Thus, S-opsin enrichment in the ventral retina better detects short-wavelength light from the sky, and M-opsin in the dorsal retina perceives the ground (e.g., a grassy field) (Baden et al., 2013; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004; Osorio and Vorobyev, 2005; Szél et al., 1992), while co-expression of both opsins (herein either mixed cones or M+S+) (Röhlich et al., 1994) broadens the spectral range of individual cones and improves perception under varying conditions of ambient light (Chang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Röhlich et al., 1994; Chang et al., 2013).

claim: True S-cones were previously thought to be evenly distributed across the retina.
source: These true S-cones are thought to be evenly distributed across the retina (Franke et al., 2019; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Szatko et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011) and to be critical for encoding color, especially in the dorsal retina where they are quasi-evenly distributed in a sea of cones expressing only M-opsin (M+S-), a pattern akin to mammalian retinas in general (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about previous understanding, supported by citations (Franke et al., 2019; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Szatko et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: True S-cones are critical for encoding color.
source: These true S-cones are thought to be evenly distributed across the retina (Franke et al., 2019; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Szatko et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011) and to be critical for encoding color, especially in the dorsal retina where they are quasi-evenly distributed in a sea of cones expressing only M-opsin (M+S-), a pattern akin to mammalian retinas in general (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Franke et al., 2019; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Szatko et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: Color-opponent retinal ganglion cells are more abundant in the dorsal-ventral transition zone.
source: Nonetheless, subsequent physiological studies revealed that color-opponent retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are more abundant in the dorsal-ventral transition zone (Chang et al., 2013) and the ventral retina (Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Chang et al., 2013).

claim: Color-opponent retinal ganglion cells are more abundant in the ventral retina.
source: Nonetheless, subsequent physiological studies revealed that color-opponent retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are more abundant in the dorsal-ventral transition zone (Chang et al., 2013) and the ventral retina (Joesch and Meister, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Joesch and Meister, 2016).

claim: Color opponent cells are mostly located in the ventral retina according to large scale two-photon imaging results.
source: Recent large scale two-photon imaging results further demonstrated that color opponent cells were mostly located in the ventral retina (Szatko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Szatko et al., 2019).

claim: Mouse ability to distinguish color is restricted to the ventral retina.
source: Intriguingly, a behavior-based mouse study demonstrated that their ability to distinguish color is also restricted to the ventral retina (Denman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Denman et al., 2018).

claim: M-opsin expressing cones were relatively evenly distributed across dorsal, medial, and ventral retinal regions in pigmented mice.
source: As demonstrated in examples of opsin labeling from dorsal, medial, and ventral retinal areas of the pigmented mouse (Figure 1B, left), while M opsin-expressing cones (M+: M+S+ + M+S-) were relatively evenly distributed across three regions, S opsin-expressing cones (S+: M+S+ + S+M-) showed considerable anisotropy, with a high density in the ventral retina and a precipitous drop in the dorsal retina, confirming previous observations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).

claim: S-opsin expressing cones showed considerable anisotropy, with high density in the ventral retina and a precipitous drop in the dorsal retina.
source: As demonstrated in examples of opsin labeling from dorsal, medial, and ventral retinal areas of the pigmented mouse (Figure 1B, left), while M opsin-expressing cones (M+: M+S+ + M+S-) were relatively evenly distributed across three regions, S opsin-expressing cones (S+: M+S+ + S+M-) showed considerable anisotropy, with a high density in the ventral retina and a precipitous drop in the dorsal retina, confirming previous observations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and citations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).

claim: M+S- cones were concentrated in the dorsal retina of pigmented mice.
source: In addition, M+S--cones were concentrated in the dorsal retina, whereas mixed cones dominated the medial and ventral retina (Figure 1C left and Figure 2A, left column, 4th and 5th rows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2A.

claim: Mixed cones dominated the medial and ventral retina in pigmented mice.
source: In addition, M+S--cones were concentrated in the dorsal retina, whereas mixed cones dominated the medial and ventral retina (Figure 1C left and Figure 2A, left column, 4th and 5th rows).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 2A.

claim: Albino retinas had slightly smaller cone populations compared to pigmented mice.
source: Overall, albino retinas had slightly smaller cone populations (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1B; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1B, and citation (Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).

claim: M-opsin expressing cones had similar distributions in both pigmented and albino strains.
source: Interestingly, while M-opsin expressing cones had similar distributions in both strains, S-opsin expression extended well into the dorsal retina of the albino mouse, exhibiting a greatly reduced gradient of S-opsin expression toward the dorsal retina compared to that seen in pigmented mice (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A second row; Applebury et al., 2000; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1B-C and 2A.

claim: S-opsin expression extended well into the dorsal retina of the albino mouse.
source: Interestingly, while M-opsin expressing cones had similar distributions in both strains, S-opsin expression extended well into the dorsal retina of the albino mouse, exhibiting a greatly reduced gradient of S-opsin expression toward the dorsal retina compared to that seen in pigmented mice (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A second row; Applebury et al., 2000; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1B-C and 2A, and citations (Applebury et al., 2000; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).

claim: Albino mice exhibited a greatly reduced gradient of S-opsin expression toward the dorsal retina compared to pigmented mice.
source: Interestingly, while M-opsin expressing cones had similar distributions in both strains, S-opsin expression extended well into the dorsal retina of the albino mouse, exhibiting a greatly reduced gradient of S-opsin expression toward the dorsal retina compared to that seen in pigmented mice (Figure 1B–C, Figure 2A second row; Applebury et al., 2000; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1B-C and 2A, and citations (Applebury et al., 2000; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014).

claim: Most cones in the dorsal retina of albino mice were mixed cones.
source: Consequently, most cones in the dorsal retina were mixed cones, and M+S- cones were very sparse (7%, compared to 97% in pigmented mouse, Figure 1C right, Supplementary file 1A, Figure 2A right).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1A, and Figure 2A.

claim: M+S- cones were very sparse (7%) in the dorsal retina of albino mice, compared to 97% in pigmented mice.
source: Consequently, most cones in the dorsal retina were mixed cones, and M+S- cones were very sparse (7%, compared to 97% in pigmented mouse, Figure 1C right, Supplementary file 1A, Figure 2A right).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1A, and Figure 2A.

claim: The percentage and distribution of true S-cones were remarkably conserved between pigmented and albino strains.
source: However, despite these differences, the percentage and distribution of true S-cones were remarkably conserved between strains.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figures 1C, 2A, and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: In both pigmented and albino strains, true S-cones were extremely sparse (1%) in the dorsal retina.
source: In both strains, true S-cones were extremely sparse in the dorsal retina (1%) but highly concentrated in the ventral retina (33% vs 29%, Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: In both pigmented and albino strains, true S-cones were highly concentrated in the ventral retina (33% vs 29%).
source: In both strains, true S-cones were extremely sparse in the dorsal retina (1%) but highly concentrated in the ventral retina (33% vs 29%, Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Supplementary file 1A.

claim: The density maps of true S-cones are nearly identical in both pigmented and albino strains.
source: Notably, the density maps of true S-cones are nearly identical in both strains (Figure 2A, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by visual comparison of density maps shown in Figure 2A.

claim: True S-cone profiles were similar between pigmented and albino strains in all quadrants, except for a slightly increased density along the edge of the ventronasal quadrant in pigmented mice.
source: However, true S-cone profiles (magenta lines) were similar between the two strains in all quadrants, except for a slightly increased density along the edge of the ventronasal (VN) quadrant in pigmented mice.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SCBCs were previously identified among other bipolar, amacrine and ganglion cells in a Thy1-Clomeleon mouse line.
source: Previously, SCBCs have only been identified among other bipolar, amacrine and ganglion cells in a Thy1-Clomeleon mouse line, rendering the quantification of their distribution across the entire retina impractical (Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Haverkamp et al., 2005).

claim: A Copine9-Venus mouse line was generated in which SCBCs are specifically marked.
source: We generated a Copine9-Venus mouse line, in which SCBCs are specifically marked (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), owing to the fact that Cpne9 is an SCBC-enriched gene (Shekhar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by citation (Shekhar et al., 2016) and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Cpne9 is an SCBC-enriched gene.
source: We generated a Copine9-Venus mouse line, in which SCBCs are specifically marked (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), owing to the fact that Cpne9 is an SCBC-enriched gene (Shekhar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Shekhar et al., 2016).

claim: Venus+ bipolar cells have axon terminals narrowly ramified in sub-lamina 5 of IPL.
source: In retinal sections, these Venus+ bipolar cells have axon terminals narrowly ramified in sub-lamina 5 of IPL (Figure 3A), closely resembling type 9 BCs as identified in EM reconstructions (Behrens et al., 2016; Stabio et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and citations (Behrens et al., 2016; Stabio et al., 2018a).

claim: Venus+ bipolar cells closely resemble type 9 BCs as identified in EM reconstructions.
source: In retinal sections, these Venus+ bipolar cells have axon terminals narrowly ramified in sub-lamina 5 of IPL (Figure 3A), closely resembling type 9 BCs as identified in EM reconstructions (Behrens et al., 2016; Stabio et al., 2018a).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Behrens et al., 2016; Stabio et al., 2018a).

claim: SCBCs often extend long dendrites to reach true S-cones, bypassing other cone types.
source: In flat-mount view, these bipolar cells are often seen to extend long dendrites to reach true S-cones, bypassing other cone types (Figure 3B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The majority of SCBC dendritic endings formed enlarged terminals beneath true S-cone pedicles.
source: The majority of dendritic endings formed enlarged terminals beneath true S-cones pedicles (Figure 3C–c'), but occasional slender 'blind' endings were present (arrow in Figure 3C–c"), which have been documented for S-cone bipolar cells in many species (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Herr et al., 2003; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-c' and citations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Herr et al., 2003; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992).

claim: Occasional slender 'blind' endings were present in SCBC dendrites.
source: The majority of dendritic endings formed enlarged terminals beneath true S-cones pedicles (Figure 3C–c'), but occasional slender 'blind' endings were present (arrow in Figure 3C–c"), which have been documented for S-cone bipolar cells in many species (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Herr et al., 2003; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C-c" and citations (Haverkamp et al., 2005; Herr et al., 2003; Kouyama and Marshak, 1992).

claim: The distribution of SCBCs was skewed toward ventronasal retina, albeit with a shallower gradient than true S-cones.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that the distribution of SCBCs was also skewed toward VN retina, albeit with a shallower gradient (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: In the dorsal retina, a single true S-cone connected to approximately 4 SCBCs (3.8 ± 0.2).
source: While in the dorsal retina, a single true S-cone connected to approximately 4 SCBCs (3.8 ± 0.2, see material and methods), in the ventral retina, a single SCBC contacted approximately 5 true S-cones (4.6 ± 0.4; Figure 3C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the ventral retina, a single SCBC contacted approximately 5 true S-cones (4.6 ± 0.4).
source: While in the dorsal retina, a single true S-cone connected to approximately 4 SCBCs (3.8 ± 0.2, see material and methods), in the ventral retina, a single SCBC contacted approximately 5 true S-cones (4.6 ± 0.4; Figure 3C, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary file 2.

claim: In the dorsal retina, the true S-cone to SCBC ratio was approximately 1:3.6.
source: Specifically, in the dorsal retina, the true S-cone to SCBC ratio was approximately 1:3.6, compared to 5.3:1 in the ventral retina (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: In the ventral retina, the true S-cone to SCBC ratio was 5.3:1.
source: Specifically, in the dorsal retina, the true S-cone to SCBC ratio was approximately 1:3.6, compared to 5.3:1 in the ventral retina (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claim: There is a prevalent divergence of true S-cone to SCBC connections in the dorsal retina.
source: Accordingly, both data sets support the presence of a prevalent divergence of true S-cone to SCBC connections in the dorsal retina, in comparison to a prominent convergence of contacts from true S-cones to SCBCs in VN retina.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on connectivity data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary files 2-3.

claim: There is a prominent convergence of contacts from true S-cones to SCBCs in ventronasal retina.
source: Accordingly, both data sets support the presence of a prevalent divergence of true S-cone to SCBC connections in the dorsal retina, in comparison to a prominent convergence of contacts from true S-cones to SCBCs in VN retina.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on connectivity data shown in Figure 3C and Supplementary files 2-3.

claim: The specificity of wiring from true S-cones to SCBCs confirms the identity of true S-cones as revealed by opsin labeling.
source: Critically, the specificity of wiring from true S-cones to SCBCs also confirms the identity of true S-cones as revealed by opsin labeling and further supports the finding that true S-cones are highly concentrated in VN mouse retina.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the connectivity data shown in Figure 3.

claim: True S-cones in the ventral retina appeared to cluster together rather than forming an even distribution.
source: Intriguingly, we discovered in both strains that true S-cones in the ventral retina appeared to cluster together rather than forming an even distribution, as revealed by K-nearest neighbor analysis (Figure 4A–B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by K-nearest neighbor analysis shown in Figure 4A-B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: True S-cone clustering may increase the availability of targets for individual SCBCs in a reduced space.
source: Ideally, such true S-cone clustering may increase the availability of targets for individual SCBCs in a reduced space.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed clustering pattern.

claim: True S-cone placement was quite irregular and nearly indistinguishable from shuffled populations.
source: Interestingly, far from being regularly distributed, true S-cone placement was quite irregular and nearly indistinguishable from shuffled populations (including a slight trend toward regularity measures lower than random, which may indicate a tendency toward clustering, Figure 4D; see Reese, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by regularity index analysis shown in Figure 4D and citation (Reese, 2008).

claim: S-cone neighbor ratios (SCNRs) were significantly larger for true S-cones than for other cone types, especially in ventral retinas.
source: Intriguingly, SCNRs were significantly larger for true S-cones than for other cone types, which were equal to expected ratios due to random chance—especially so in ventral retinas, further indicating a clustering of true S-cones in those areas (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by SCNR analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: A more extreme form of clustering of S-cones has been observed in the 'wild' mouse.
source: Notably, a more extreme form of clustering of S-cones has been observed in the 'wild' mouse (Warwick et al., 2018) and with much lower densities in some felids (Ahnelt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Warwick et al., 2018; Ahnelt et al., 2000).

claim: Clustering of S-cones with much lower densities has been observed in some felids.
source: Notably, a more extreme form of clustering of S-cones has been observed in the 'wild' mouse (Warwick et al., 2018) and with much lower densities in some felids (Ahnelt et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Ahnelt et al., 2000).

claim: True S-cone clustering may reflect the mode of true S-cone development in the ventral retina, for example, by 'clonal expansion' to achieve unusually high densities.
source: Here, such clustering may reflect the mode of true S-cone development in the ventral retina, for example, by 'clonal expansion' to achieve unusually high densities (Bruhn and Cepko, 1996; Reese et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations (Bruhn and Cepko, 1996; Reese et al., 1999).

claim: True S-cone clustering may facilitate the wiring of true S-cones with sparsely distributed SCBCs.
source: It is tempting to speculate that it may also facilitate the wiring of true S-cones with sparsely distributed SCBCs, which were not observed to cluster in the ventral retina (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed patterns shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SCBCs were not observed to cluster in the ventral retina.
source: It is tempting to speculate that it may also facilitate the wiring of true S-cones with sparsely distributed SCBCs, which were not observed to cluster in the ventral retina (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Groups of true S-cones form clusters whose pedicles in the OPL were tightly congregated in a patch and contacted by a nearby SCBC.
source: Indeed, we observed examples of groups of true S-cones forming clusters whose pedicles in the OPL were tightly congregated in a patch and contacted by a nearby SCBC (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mice can detect color despite being nocturnal and having a rod-dominated retina.
source: Despite being nocturnal and having a rod-dominated retina (Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979; Jeon et al., 1998), mice can detect color (Denman et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Carter-Dawson and LaVail, 1979; Jeon et al., 1998; Denman et al., 2018; Jacobs et al., 2004).

claim: True S-cones provide short-wavelength signals for color discrimination.
source: Although it remains uncertain whether the source of long-wavelength sensitive signals for color opponency arises in rods or M-cones (Baden and Osorio, 2019; Ekesten et al., 2000; Ekesten and Gouras, 2005; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Reitner et al., 1991), it is clear that true S-cones provide short-wavelength signals for color discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Baden and Osorio, 2019; Ekesten et al., 2000; Ekesten and Gouras, 2005; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Reitner et al., 1991).

claim: It remains uncertain whether the source of long-wavelength sensitive signals for color opponency arises in rods or M-cones.
source: Although it remains uncertain whether the source of long-wavelength sensitive signals for color opponency arises in rods or M-cones (Baden and Osorio, 2019; Ekesten et al., 2000; Ekesten and Gouras, 2005; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Reitner et al., 1991), it is clear that true S-cones provide short-wavelength signals for color discrimination.
evidence: This is supported by citations (Baden and Osorio, 2019; Ekesten et al., 2000; Ekesten and Gouras, 2005; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Reitner et al., 1991).

claim: The discovery of high enrichment of true S-cones in the ventral retina provides a previously missed anatomical feature for mouse color vision.
source: Thus, our discovery of high enrichment of true S-cones in the ventral retina provides a previously missed anatomical feature for mouse color vision that could help to re-interpret these results.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the anatomical findings presented in the study.

claim: High ventral true S-cone density will provide a much higher sensitivity of short-wavelength signals, thus facilitating color detection for the upper visual field.
source: From projections mapping true S-cone densities into visual space (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Sterratt et al., 2013), it is conceivable that high ventral true S-cone density will provide a much higher sensitivity of short-wavelength signals, thus facilitating color detection for the upper visual field.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and citation (Sterratt et al., 2013).

claim: True S-cone signals carried by SCBCs in the dorsal retina might participate in non-image forming vision.
source: Although the true S-cone signals carried by SCBCs in the dorsal retina might not be significant for color detection, they could certainly participate in other functions, such as non-image forming vision, that are known to involve short-wavelength signals (Altimus et al., 2008; Doyle et al., 2008; Patterson et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations (Altimus et al., 2008; Doyle et al., 2008; Patterson et al., 2020).

claim: The overall true S-cone percentage in the mouse retina remains approximately 10%.
source: Interestingly, the overall true S-cone percentage in the mouse retina remains approximately 10% (Figure 2B), and the average true S-cone to SCBC ratio across the whole retina is about 1.7:1 (Supplementary file 1B-C), similar to what has been reported in other mammals (Ahnelt et al., 2006; Ahnelt and Kolb, 2000; Bumsted et al., 1997; Bumsted and Hendrickson, 1999; Curcio et al., 1991; Hendrickson and Hicks, 2002; Hunt and Peichl, 2014; Kryger et al., 1998; Lukáts et al., 2005; Müller and Peichl, 1989; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2010; Peichl et al., 2000; Schiviz et al., 2008; Shinozaki et al., 2010; Szél et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and citations to other mammalian studies.

claim: The average true S-cone to SCBC ratio across the whole retina is about 1.7:1.
source: Interestingly, the overall true S-cone percentage in the mouse retina remains approximately 10% (Figure 2B), and the average true S-cone to SCBC ratio across the whole retina is about 1.7:1 (Supplementary file 1B-C), similar to what has been reported in other mammals (Ahnelt et al., 2006; Ahnelt and Kolb, 2000; Bumsted et al., 1997; Bumsted and Hendrickson, 1999; Curcio et al., 1991; Hendrickson and Hicks, 2002; Hunt and Peichl, 2014; Kryger et al., 1998; Lukáts et al., 2005; Müller and Peichl, 1989; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2010; Peichl et al., 2000; Schiviz et al., 2008; Shinozaki et al., 2010; Szél et al., 1988).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Supplementary file 1B-C and citations to other mammalian studies.

claim: The spatial rearrangement of true S-cones and SCBCs likely reflects evolutionary adaptation to enhance short-wavelength signaling and color coding for the upper visual field.
source: Such a spatial rearrangement of true S-cones and SCBCs likely reflects evolutionary adaptation to enhance short-wavelength signaling and color coding for the upper visual field as best suited for the habitat and behavior of mice (Baden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative evolutionary interpretation supported by citation (Baden et al., 2020).

claim: The spatial arrangement may facilitate aerial predator detection during daytime.
source: For example, it may facilitate aerial predator detection during daytime (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citation (Yilmaz and Meister, 2013).

claim: Skewed S-cone arrangement has been reported for other terrestrial prey mammals.
source: Similarly, skewed S-cone arrangement has been reported for other terrestrial prey mammals (Famiglietti and Sharpe, 1995; Juliusson et al., 1994; Röhlich et al., 1994), while zebrafish possess a UV-enriched ventral retina that enhances their predation (Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Famiglietti and Sharpe, 1995; Juliusson et al., 1994; Röhlich et al., 1994).

claim: Zebrafish possess a UV-enriched ventral retina that enhances their predation.
source: Similarly, skewed S-cone arrangement has been reported for other terrestrial prey mammals (Famiglietti and Sharpe, 1995; Juliusson et al., 1994; Röhlich et al., 1994), while zebrafish possess a UV-enriched ventral retina that enhances their predation (Zimmermann et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Zimmermann et al., 2018).

claim: The clustering of true S-cones in the ventral retina may allow several neighboring cones of the same type to converge onto the same SCBC, which could potentially enhance signal-to-noise ratios for more accurate detection.
source: In addition, we observed that the clustering of true S-cones in the ventral retina may allow several neighboring cones of the same type to converge onto the same SCBC (Figure 4F), which could potentially enhance signal-to-noise ratios for more accurate detection, as described recently in human fovea (Schmidt et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on data shown in Figure 4F and supported by citation (Schmidt et al., 2019).

claim: Despite very different S-opsin expression patterns in both mouse strains, the true S-cone population and distribution are strikingly similar between pigmented and albino mice.
source: It is also remarkable that despite the very different S-opsin expression patterns in both mouse strains, the true S-cone population and distribution are strikingly similar between pigmented and albino mice, suggesting a common functional significance.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the comparative data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The similarity in true S-cone population and distribution between pigmented and albino mice suggests a common functional significance.
source: It is also remarkable that despite the very different S-opsin expression patterns in both mouse strains, the true S-cone population and distribution are strikingly similar between pigmented and albino mice, suggesting a common functional significance.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the comparative data.

claim: The increased density of SCBCs in the ventral retina does not match that of true S-cones.
source: However, the increased density of SCBCs in the ventral retina does not match that of true S-cones (compare Figure 3D and Figure 2a, last row).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 2A.

claim: Individual SCBCs in the ventral retina may be required to develop more dendrites to maximize the number of contacts made with different S-cone terminals.
source: Thus, individual SCBCs in the ventral retina may be required to develop more dendrites to maximize the number of contacts made with different S-cone terminals (Supplementary file 2, graphs in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data shown in Supplementary file 2 and Figure 3C.

claim: A highly reliable algorithm was developed to automatically quantify the different opsins and cone types based on high-resolution images of entire flat-mount retinas.
source: We developed a highly reliable algorithm to automatically quantify the different opsins (S and M) and cone types (M+S-, true S, and mixed cones, Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) based on high-resolution images of entire flat-mount retinas immunolabeled with S- and M-opsin antibodies (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological claim supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The automatic quantification algorithm was validated by statistical comparison with manual counting (Pearson correlation coefficient R2 = 96–99% for M- or S-opsin respectively).
source: This automation was validated by statistical comparison with manual counting performed by an experienced investigator (Pearson correlation coefficient R2 = 96–99% for M- or S-opsin respectively, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by validation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Venus-Cpne9 mouse line carries a reporter (Venus) allele under the control of the mouse Cpne9 locus.
source: The Venus-Cpne9 mouse line (n = 5; based on previous single cell sequencing data [Shekhar et al., 2016]) carries a reporter (Venus) allele under the control of the mouse Cpne9 locus.
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation (Shekhar et al., 2016).

claim: The reporter allele was created directly in B6.SJL(F1) zygotes using CRISPR-mediated homologous recombination.
source: The reporter allele was created directly in B6.SJL(F1) zygotes using CRISPR-mediated homologous recombination (HR) (Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological description supported by citation (Yang et al., 2013).

claim: 11 out of 15 F0 live births were found to carry the knockin allele by homologous recombination, a HR rate of 73%.
source: With a total of 15 F0 live births from 6 pseudopregnant females, 11 were found to carry the knockin allele by homologous recombination, a HR rate of 73%.
evidence: This is a methodological result describing the efficiency of the genetic modification.

claim: Luminance detection can occur across the mouse retina.
source: However, previous physiological and behavioral studies indicate that, although luminance detection can occur across the mouse retina, color discrimination is restricted to the ventral retina (Breuninger et al., 2011; Denman et al., 2018; Szatko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Breuninger et al., 2011; Denman et al., 2018; Szatko et al., 2019).

claim: Color discrimination is restricted to the ventral retina.
source: However, previous physiological and behavioral studies indicate that, although luminance detection can occur across the mouse retina, color discrimination is restricted to the ventral retina (Breuninger et al., 2011; Denman et al., 2018; Szatko et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations (Breuninger et al., 2011; Denman et al., 2018; Szatko et al., 2019).

claim: M-opsin antibody signals did not label cone structures other than their outer segments.
source: Because M-opsin antibody signals did not label cone structures other than their outer segments, we first identified true S-cones at the outer segment level and then traced S-opsin labeling to their pedicles in the outer plexiform layer (OPL), where they connect with SCBCs (Figure 3C, for more details see material and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological observation.

claim: True S-cone pedicles contain either low or no cone arrestin.
source: To verify connectivity between Venus+ SCBC dendrites and true S-cone pedicles in the OPL, in addition to S-opsin immunodetection, we also labeled retinas using cone arrestin antibodies to discriminate mixed cone pedicles from true S-cone pedicles, because true S-cone pedicles contain either low or no cone arrestin (Figure 3B, Haverkamp et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and citation (Haverkamp et al., 2005).

claim: Convergent as well as divergent connections were found between true S-cones and SCBCs in both dorsal and ventral retina.
source: Although convergent as well divergent connections were found between true S-cones and SCBCs in both dorsal and ventral retina (see the source data), we noted different connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is supported by connectivity data referenced in the text.

claim: The gradients of S- and M-opsin expression along the dorsal-ventral axis have been well documented in mouse retina.
source: In mouse retina, the gradients of S- and M-opsin expression along the dorsal-ventral axis have been well documented (Figure 1A–B; Applebury et al., 2000; Calderone and Jacobs, 1995; Chang et al., 2013; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Lyubarsky et al., 1999; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Szél et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2011), but the distribution of individual cone types with different combinations of opsin expression across the whole retina has not been characterized (but see Baden et al., 2013; Eldred et al., 2020), which we discuss below).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations (Applebury et al., 2000; Calderone and Jacobs, 1995; Chang et al., 2013; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Lyubarsky et al., 1999; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Szél et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2011).

claim: The distribution of individual cone types with different combinations of opsin expression across the whole retina has not been characterized prior to this study.
source: In mouse retina, the gradients of S- and M-opsin expression along the dorsal-ventral axis have been well documented (Figure 1A–B; Applebury et al., 2000; Calderone and Jacobs, 1995; Chang et al., 2013; Haverkamp et al., 2005; Jelcick et al., 2011; Lyubarsky et al., 1999; Ortín-Martínez et al., 2014; Szél et al., 1992; Wang et al., 2011), but the distribution of individual cone types with different combinations of opsin expression across the whole retina has not been characterized (but see Baden et al., 2013; Eldred et al., 2020), which we discuss below).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the current study, with acknowledgment of related work (Baden et al., 2013; Eldred et al., 2020).

claim: A recent study successfully modeled cone opsin expression and type determination according to graded thyroid hormone signaling in a pigmented mouse strain (C57BL/6).
source: A recent study successfully modeled cone opsin expression and type determination according to graded thyroid hormone signaling in a pigmented mouse strain (C57BL/6) (Eldred et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation (Eldred et al., 2020).

claim: Topographic representation of the visual world in the brain originates from the light-sensitive photoreceptors in the retina.
source: Topographic representation of the visual world in the brain originates from the light-sensitive photoreceptors in the retina (Rhim et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Rhim et al., 2017).

claim: The numbers and distributions of photoreceptors vary considerably among different vertebrates.
source: Although the neuronal architecture of the retina is similar among different vertebrates, the numbers and distributions of photoreceptors vary considerably (Hunt and Peichl, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation (Hunt and Peichl, 2014).

claim: Photoreceptor patterns have been evolutionarily selected, adapting to the animal's unique behavior and lifestyle.
source: Such patterns have been evolutionarily selected, adapting to the animal's unique behavior (diurnal or nocturnal) and lifestyle (prey or predator) for better use of the visual information in the natural environment (Dominy and Lucas, 2001; Gerl and Morris, 2008; Peichl, 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Dominy and Lucas, 2001; Gerl and Morris, 2008; Peichl, 2005).

claim: Trichromatic color vision is privileged for some primates amongst mammals.
source: While amongst mammals, trichromatic color vision is privileged for some primates (Jacobs et al., 1996; Nathans et al., 1986; Yokoyama and Yokoyama, 1989), most terrestrial mammals are dichromatic (Marshak and Mills, 2014; Puller and Haverkamp, 2011; Jacobs, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Jacobs et al., 1996; Nathans et al., 1986; Yokoyama and Yokoyama, 1989).

claim: Most terrestrial mammals are dichromatic.
source: While amongst mammals, trichromatic color vision is privileged for some primates (Jacobs et al., 1996; Nathans et al., 1986; Yokoyama and Yokoyama, 1989), most terrestrial mammals are dichromatic (Marshak and Mills, 2014; Puller and Haverkamp, 2011; Jacobs, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Marshak and Mills, 2014; Puller and Haverkamp, 2011; Jacobs, 1993).
